Renewable Energy boom crashes in South Africa - whats at stake?

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa's renewable energy (RE) programme has been lauded as one of the most successful internationally. Over the three bidding rounds, the cost of renewable energy has consistently dropped and now wind and solar energy is cheaper than coal fired energy. It has attracted R195-billion in foreign investment, created 29 888 jobs in construction and seen manufacturing development in parts of the country that were desperately neglected.
The RE programme was set to continue until 2030 with a focus on local procurement of up to 60% in round 4. In the light of this, the Renewable Energy Technology Centre was established at the Cape Peninsula University of Technology, CPUT, to provide skills to the industry. Wind turbine plants were built at Atlantis in the Western Cape and Coega Industrial in Port Elizabeth. The Northern and Eastern Cape have been the biggest growth areas, creating employment and social upliftment in areas of the country that are desperately under-developed with massive unemployment.
One of the most important elements of the Renewable Energy contracts is that written into any commission is a 20 year commitment to social and economic investment into the communities within a 50 kilometre radius of the plants. The community trusts are a one third shareholder of every plant. R13.4-billion has already been invested into communities, creating infrastructure in places where the government was unable to provide. Essential areas for development like school teachers, health services and various social upliftment programs are being funded. Over the next 20 years, R6-billion rand will continue to go into these communities in dividends. Renewable Energy companies don’t establish social upliftment programmes, but invest in the NGOs that are already established in those areas.



Summary:
Jeffreys Bay – the iconic surf mecca famous for its powerful winds - saw the first wind farm to be built in the Eastern Cape as part of round one. They brought in the turbines from overseas. Since then 16 wind farms have been developed across the Eastern Cape with several more planned as part of round 4.
DCD Wind tower manufacturing plant is an entirely SA-owned firm and was established in the Coega Industrial Development Zone to supply wind towers for the wind farms commissioned in round 3, with the knowledge that round 4 would provide work for the next 10 years. They invested R400-million in establishing the factory and employed 172 people, many of whom found work for the first time in their lives. When round 4 was delayed, they downscaled to 135 core workers. The last tower left the factory in November 2016. Workers have been sitting at home on short pay for the last five months. Everyone was holding their breath after President Zuma promised in his SONA 2017 speech that the IPP agreements would be signed. The date set was the 10th April - that date has come and gone and nobody knows when they will be signed. The shareholders can’t hold out forever.
Whole technical teams across the Eastern Cape who moved from one wind project to the next with the promise of work till 2027 have been laid off. Wind farm Project Manager Nico Schneider relocated to the Eastern Cape. He was told this week by the investors that “Renewable Energy is dead in South Africa”. They are moving elsewhere.
The entire future of a boom industry of development, of manufacturing, technical skills development, employment and potential social investment hangs in the balance.

Press Release:


Windfarms
South Africa's Renewable Energy (RE) programme was lauded as one of the most successful internationally. It attracted billions in direct foreign
investment, with renewable energy plants being built in some of the most desperately neglected parts of the country. Thousands of jobs in
construction and manufacturing were also created. Now, with major delays in the fourth phase of the programme, the entire future of renewable
energy in South Africa, hangs in the balance. Carte Blanche investigates.

Script:


Script: Lindile Bisho has been sitting at home for the last 6 months anxiously waiting for news about when he could possibly return to work.
Lindile “Ja it’s been a stressful 6 months, It’s been hardship of hardship one has kids that are going to school
Script: At 37 he got his first formal job at DCD Wind Tower manufacturing in Port Elizabeth supporting his own family of 6 as well as his siblings in the rural areas.
Link 01 00 31 03 The national unemployment figures make for depressing reading and even more so here in the Eastern Cape the renewable energy sector for a brief moment was providing a glimmer of hope
Script: Driving through the Eastern Cape you are struck by the boom in renewable energy power plants, there are 15 wind farms here, 10 more in the Western Cape and, fields of solar power- in the Northern Cape, South Africa is prime renewable energy country bringing work to the rural areas.
Link “Globally green energy is expected to grow by a massive 33% a year for the next five years and in that context the SA renewable energy program is considered one of the finest of it’s kind
Script: Mark Pickering M.D. of Jeffreys Bay Wind farm which was the first in South African
Mark Pickering “we had no history of renewable plants we had no history of private investment in the power sector to being one of the leaders globally until recently
Script: South Africa followed the global trend investing in green energy in 2010 with the independent power producer procurement program, to date 3 rounds have been commission and delivered and with each round the electricity price dropped by 68%. Renewables are now cheaper than new coal and nuclear.
Mark Pickering ”It has been described as the 4th industrial revolution the decline in cost in renewable energy worldwide is going to fundamentally change the world there is no way SA is going to escape that revolution “
Script: Over the last 4 years there was a boom in construction, suppliers, manufacturing plants and training facilities. But for the last two years Eskom has held this thriving industry to ransom grinding it to a standstill by not signing the power purchases agreements for round 4 and people like Lindela and Zuka Majiba are the casualties
Zuko 01 00 31 12 It’s frustrating because I am sitting at home doing nothing
Links: 01 00 00 As part of the renewable program Government identified two so called development nodes one in Atlantis in the Western Cape and the other here at Coega outside Port Elizabeth now this impressive half a billion rand factory is a result of that forward thinking sadly though for the past few months it’s been standing idle
Alta Mari 09 27 45 19 the power purchase agreements is what our life line is in this factory we need to get them signed to get the contracts going
Script: Managing director Alta Marie Gerber was on the ground from the outset, and along with Zuko, Lindela and 177 other they built a thriving plant
Alta Mari 09 41 02 15 The demand for towers or sections are way bigger than I and the factory in CT can supply, so there would have been work for the next 5 years and that’s just from the round 4 PPA’s
Script: The last wind tower left the factory in November 2016, all prospective orders were frozen. Zuko along with the rest of the work force has been on short time since January. He is devastated because he moved to DCD from Volkswagen, because he saw wind turbines as the future.
Zuko 09 59 36 09 We are struggling already if you look at the Eastern Cape …. there are a lot of people who are unemployed and then you start to think about yourself is it possible that you are going to get a job if this place get closed
Lindele 10 34 33 10 my salary not only helps my family alone because you will find that there is an old woman selling paraffin around the corner another one has got a stand where they sell vegetables so my salary goes a long way in helping other people around my community as well
Script: DCD Wind Towers is just one of many companies that are at risk explains Brenda Martin Chair of the SA Renewable Energy Council
Brenda 01 07 16 07 What really concerns me at the moment is the number of local companies that are having to close their doors as a result of this ongoing delay we have companies that have employed SA and most of the people employed are in rural areas … you have youth that have been trained you have construction that has skilled up to provide construction services all of those businesses are left to do something else I don’t know what.
Script: By April 2015, 64 renewable projects had been completed, and there’re 37 preferred bidders in round 4 kicking their heels
Mark Pickering 05 14 18 18 there was about 1000 MW a year being commissioned and for the last 2 years nothing, so in rand terms the fourth window we think is about R58 billion rand that is forgone investment opportunity at this stage
Script: In our struggling economy Renewables was the biggest attracter of foreign investment responsible for 85% of all direct foreign investment last year generating over 26000 jobs
Brenda 04 45 04 19 so many industries are losing jobs and here we have an industry that is gaining jobs… why would we as a country turn down or turn off a tap which is flowing so beautifully.
Script: We asked energy specialist Prof Anton Eberhard of UCT’s Graduate School of Business what he thought was behind the delays
Anton “Eskom is trying to protect its market position its acting like any monopolist would its concerned that increasingly independent power producers are competitive and so it’s trying to restrict their entry. The renewable energy IPP program was not only successful in bringing in private investment 190 Billion over 4 years or 92 projects but it’s been entirely devoid of any corruption allegations it’s probably the most transparent government private procurement that we ever had and so this rent seeking elite don’t see the equivalent opportunities for corruption in the renewable energy program as they do within Eskom
Script: In February everyone thought the impasse was over. In his state of the nation speech, President Jacob Zuma committed to the renewable energy program
ZUMA SONA Eskom will sign the outstanding power purchase agreements for renewable energy
Script: But there were other political forces at play, the Coal Truck drivers came out in force after being fed misinformation about the cost of renewables and the imminent closure of mines
Anton 08 58 37 03 Eskom is using less coal because it’s selling less electricity it also talked about immediate closing of power stations and that’s not scheduled until the 2020’s so clearly this was political, this was mobilising a constituency against renewable energy for particular purposes
Script: Eskom is not only holding the Renewable sector to ransom but also the Department of Trade and Industry who attracted the investors and the Department of Higher Education who also threw their weight behind this boom industry.
Link: 04 30 01 08 The demand for skills in the renewable energy sector led the Department of Higher Education and Training to invest R105 million rand at the SARETEC facility here in Cape Town. It provides skills to students who rather uniquely are almost guaranteed employment by the time they qualify
Script: Managing director Naim Rassool left the private sector to develop a qualification that is recognised globally.
Naim: 03 52 20 21 This is one of 5 or 6 facilities worldwide. It’s basically the only one in the southern hemisphere what makes it really unique is that it has a Nordex live turbine that sits within the facility. Most of our students come from the rural Eastern Cape and the Western Cape so that they can then go back to the rural areas to work on the wind farms
Script: Apelele Tyali was a engineer in the navy and on a trip home to Umtata she spotted the wind turbines along the N2, with 15 wind farms already in the Eastern Cape she decided on a change of career
Apelele 04 25 17 12 “ well I am placed to do my 2 months training at Westess in Hopefield so I am hoping they will hire me after my 2 months because there are very few females in this field
Script: Sadly Aplele may well be one of the last students to benefit from this world class training institution and Naim and his staff’s funding is in the balance
Naim: 03 56 55 05 we have cancelled our next program that was going to begin the first of August because our current group of students of 15 we were only able to place 5 …SARETECH has put a stop to training further wind turbine service technicians and is not even training solar PV Technicians.
Script: Eskom says IPPS are expensive but they lump peak diesel IPPS with the rest of renewables clouding the figures. Wind power is 40% cheaper to build and deliver than new coal. Renewable plants are completed and come online within two years at no cost to the tax payer. In contrast Medupi and Kusile- 10 years in construction, 60 Billion rand over budget which Eskom secured 20 billion rand loan from China to complete.
Anton 08 52 37 03 we have a huge huge battle and restructuring any sector as large and as powerful as the electricity sector it’s not going to be easy. Its aligned and committed to an obsolete business model and it’s in this classic death spiral its able to sell every year less and less electricity and it’s still wedded to this big coal big nuclear which are the most expensive sources
Script: All inquiries to Eskom, Department of Public Enterprises and the Department of Energy referred us the Portfolio committee meeting in June which outlined 6 more steps they need put in place. It doesn’t look like the IPPs will be signed anytime soon.
Mark Pickering 05 18 17 18 at this stage it’s hard to cling onto hope I must say in the face of what really seems like irrational action by parts of government. We would at this stage rather develop in Mozambique in Zambia basically anywhere else on the continent “
Lindela. The fact that we are not being told the truth about these PPAs it’s also something that makes us very worried and loose trust in Government
John 09 37 34 22 Do you think you might be the last one to switch off the lights and move on
Alta Mari I hope not… I have been dreading the day when its coming I was the one who was so proud to put the sign onto the factory why would I want to take it down ……

metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa's renewable energy (RE) programme has been lauded as one of the most successful internationally. Over the three bidding rounds, the cost of renewable energy has consistently dropped and now wind and solar energy is cheaper than coal fired energy. It has attracted R195-billion in foreign investment, created 29 888 jobs in construction and seen manufacturing development in parts of the country that were desperately neglected. The RE programme was set to continue until 2030 with a focus on local procurement of up to 60% in round 4. In the light of this, the Renewable Energy Technology Centre was established at the Cape Peninsula University of Technology, CPUT, to provide skills to the industry. Wind turbine plants were built at Atlantis in the Western Cape and Coega Industrial in Port Elizabeth. The Northern and Eastern Cape have been the biggest growth areas, creating employment and social upliftment in areas of the country that are desperately under-developed with massive unemployment. One of the most important elements of the Renewable Energy contracts is that written into any commission is a 20 year commitment to social and economic investment into the communities within a 50 kilometre radius of the plants. The community trusts are a one third shareholder of every plant. R13.4-billion has already been invested into communities, creating infrastructure in places where the government was unable to provide. Essential areas for development like school teachers, health services and various social upliftment programs are being funded. Over the next 20 years, R6-billion rand will continue to go into these communities in dividends. Renewable Energy companies don’t establish social upliftment programmes, but invest in the NGOs that are already established in those areas.
metadata.Summary: Jeffreys Bay – the iconic surf mecca famous for its powerful winds - saw the first wind farm to be built in the Eastern Cape as part of round one. They brought in the turbines from overseas. Since then 16 wind farms have been developed across the Eastern Cape with several more planned as part of round 4. DCD Wind tower manufacturing plant is an entirely SA-owned firm and was established in the Coega Industrial Development Zone to supply wind towers for the wind farms commissioned in round 3, with the knowledge that round 4 would provide work for the next 10 years. They invested R400-million in establishing the factory and employed 172 people, many of whom found work for the first time in their lives. When round 4 was delayed, they downscaled to 135 core workers. The last tower left the factory in November 2016. Workers have been sitting at home on short pay for the last five months. Everyone was holding their breath after President Zuma promised in his SONA 2017 speech that the IPP agreements would be signed. The date set was the 10th April - that date has come and gone and nobody knows when they will be signed. The shareholders can’t hold out forever. Whole technical teams across the Eastern Cape who moved from one wind project to the next with the promise of work till 2027 have been laid off. Wind farm Project Manager Nico Schneider relocated to the Eastern Cape. He was told this week by the investors that “Renewable Energy is dead in South Africa”. They are moving elsewhere. The entire future of a boom industry of development, of manufacturing, technical skills development, employment and potential social investment hangs in the balance.
